archetype.name: Playoff Team (pass-first, turnover-prone)
archetype.definition: A team whose quarterback-driven passing game and stingy scoring defense make it a legitimate postseason side, held back from contender status by a giveaway habit and a run game that doesn't move the chains.

report.headline: Maye's arm is carrying a good team through a turnover problem.
report.take:
This is not last year's Patriots, and that is not an insult. The 2025 team went 14-3 with the league's best offense by EPA and nearly three and a half wins of luck stacked on top. This version is a tier down: 10th in net EPA, 11th on offense, 17th on defense by EPA. It is still a well-built team whose whole identity runs through Drake Maye, who has started every game. The passing offense is 7th in EPA per play while the run game is 26th, and Mike Vrabel plays it with no fear: New England has gone for it on every fourth-down chance the model flags, first in the league.

The season has two halves. In the first three weeks the offense gave the ball away in bunches, scoring 10 at Seattle with three turnovers and getting buried 35-6 in Jacksonville on a -13.9 passing EPA day. Since then the passing game has been positive every week: +11.0 in the comeback at Buffalo, +29.5 against the Raiders, +12.6 against the Jets. The losses came against a top-two defense and a top-five offense on the road. The improvement since then is the quarterback settling in, not the schedule softening.

The gap that matters is between yards and points. The offense is 7th in yards per game but 19th in scoring, and the 13 turnovers explain most of it. They have turned it over in every game, and the turnover margin per game ranks 30th. That is the biggest drag on the team and the likeliest to improve. Last year's group was 8th in turnover margin, and an offense this efficient through the air shouldn't keep giving away two a game. The defense has the opposite problem. Allowing 18.8 points a game is 5th-best, but its EPA allowed is merely average. Red-zone and third-down stops are doing a lot of the work, and those numbers tend to drift back toward the middle.

So the 4-2 record is about right. The point differential implies roughly three wins, and the turnovers make the team look worse than it plays. Bigger worries are building, though. The interior line and right tackle came out of the Jets game hurt, Romeo Doubs is on IR until after the Week 11 bye, and the No. 1 corner, Carlton Davis, is out. A Maye offense that holds the ball 3.1 seconds, second-longest in the league, behind a line already 22nd in pressure rate allowed is the pressure point for the next month.

strengths.title: Maye's passing game drives everything
strengths.body: The pass offense ranks 7th in EPA per play, and the last three weeks have each been strongly positive after a rough opening stretch. It comes from a quarterback who extends plays and pushes the ball while holding it longer than almost anyone. With Maye healthy and starting every week, this looks real and like it should hold. Last year's offense led the league with much of the same core.

strengths.title: Defense wins where points are decided
strengths.body: The defense allows the 5th-fewest points despite a 17th-ranked EPA. It closes out drives: 7th in red-zone TD rate allowed and 11th on third down, plus sound tackling, 8th in missed-tackle rate. That keeps games close even when the offense hands over field position. Situational defense is real but noisier than down-to-down efficiency, so expect the points allowed to creep up somewhat.

strengths.title: Vrabel's fourth-down aggression
strengths.body: New England has gone for it on every fourth down the model flags, the most aggressive rate in the league. With a top-tier passing offense, that turns marginal drives into points and extra possessions. It is a coaching choice, so it will stay.

concerns.title: Turnovers in every single game
concerns.body: Thirteen giveaways in six games leave New England 30th in turnover margin per game. That is why a top-10 yardage offense scores like a middling one. Some of it is the cost of an aggressive, hold-and-extend passing style. Most of it should regress toward normal, as last year's 8th-ranked margin suggests. Until it does, it caps the ceiling.

concerns.title: Run game moves yards, not chains
concerns.body: The rushing totals look healthy, but the run game ranks 26th in EPA and 23rd in success rate. The Jets game had 148 rush yards and -7.0 rush EPA. The line isn't the main culprit, with backs getting 2.8 yards before contact (8th). The problem is what happens after contact and on the downs that matter. It forces Maye to carry the offense.

concerns.title: Thin line, depleted secondary
concerns.body: Guard Vera-Tucker, right tackle Moses (seen in a walking boot) and center Ben Brown are all questionable after leaving or getting hurt against the Jets. That is a problem for a line already 22nd in pressure rate allowed protecting a quarterback who holds the ball 3.1 seconds. On the other side, Davis (95% of snaps) is out for a defense that already ranks 24th against deep passes. These are injury-driven and should be temporary, but they land on the weak spots.

trend.note: After a turnover-heavy start that included the 35-6 loss in Jacksonville, the passing game has been sharply positive three weeks running and the team hasn't lost since. The giveaways haven't stopped yet, though.

nextGame.headline: Short week at Soldier Field with a battered line
nextGame.body:
This is a matchup of strengths and holes. Chicago's pass defense is 7th in EPA, 2nd in sack rate and 2nd on third down, and it smothers short throws (3rd). It is also the worst in the league at preventing explosive passes and deep completions. That is exactly where a Maye offense that holds the ball and pushes it downfield makes its money. On the other side, Ben Johnson's offense leads the league in time of possession and runs more than expected. It runs well, 7th in yards per carry, at a New England run defense ranked 23rd in EPA. The Book has the Bears by 3 with a 50.5 total, essentially home field.

Availability tilts both ways. New England comes in on four days' rest with three offensive linemen questionable, A.J. Brown limited, Doubs on IR and Davis out at corner. Chicago is missing both Montez Sweat (suspended) and Dayo Odeyingbo (IR) off the edge, which should blunt the sack rate that makes its defense work. Linebacker T.J. Edwards and running back Kyle Monangai are also out, and guard Jonah Jackson is questionable. Both teams are 30th in turnover margin per game, so ball security could swing it either way.

waysToWin.title: Hit the Bears over the top
waysToWin.body: Chicago ranks last in explosive pass rate and deep EPA allowed, while Maye's passing game is top-10 and built on extended plays. With two edge rushers missing, Maye should get time to find the shots. Three or four explosive completions could win this on their own.

waysToWin.title: Exploit the missing pass rush
waysToWin.body: Chicago's 2nd-ranked sack rate came with Sweat and Odeyingbo, and neither plays Thursday. If the Bears can't get home with four, the third-down defense that ranks 2nd loses its main weapon. New England's patchwork line also gets a softer test than it would have.

waysToWin.title: Win the giveaway coin flip
waysToWin.body: Both teams sit 30th in turnover margin per game. New England has hidden its giveaways by holding opponents to TDs on only half of their red-zone trips. Chicago scores TDs on two-thirds of its own trips but has allowed them at a 22nd-ranked rate on defense. A clean game from Maye plus red-zone stops would tip a close game.

waysToLose.title: Bears grind the clock on the ground
waysToLose.body: Chicago leads the league in time of possession and runs efficiently, 11th in run EPA. New England's run defense ranks 23rd. Long drives shorten the game and keep Maye on the sideline, which is the script a ball-control favorite wants. Monangai's absence dents it but doesn't erase it.

waysToLose.title: Line breaks down on short rest
waysToLose.body: Three starting linemen are questionable on four days' rest, in front of a quarterback who holds the ball 3.1 seconds behind a line already 22nd in pressure rate allowed. Even without its top edges, Chicago's defense ranks 9th in pressure rate. Pressure on a patched-up interior could turn long developing plays into sacks and turnovers.

waysToLose.title: Short-field and special-teams leaks
waysToLose.body: Chicago's special teams rank 5th in EPA per game, New England's 15th. Combined with New England's turnover habit, that is how a road team gets beaten on field position without being outplayed from scrimmage. The Jacksonville blowout showed how quickly giveaways snowball.

nextGame.watch: Whether New England's three questionable linemen play, and whether Maye can get the deep shots off against a Bears defense missing both starting edge rushers.

restOfSeason.body:
The passing offense is the sustainable piece: Maye has started every game, the efficiency is top-10, and it has been trending up. The turnover margin should improve meaningfully, since nothing about this offense suggests a league-worst giveaway rate is its true level, and that alone should lift the scoring closer to what the yardage suggests. The defense will probably give back some of its points-allowed ranking, because red-zone and third-down stops have been propping up an average down-to-down unit. Davis's absence and a weak run defense are real issues.

The schedule is split. There are soft spots in two Miami games, an 0-6 Chargers team and the Jets. There are also heavy games: Buffalo at home, unbeaten Minnesota and Kansas City, plus Detroit and Green Bay. Doubs's return after the bye and the line's health decide how well this offense holds up through that stretch. This looks like a double-digit-win wild-card team that can still challenge Buffalo for the division if the giveaways dry up.
swingFactors: Offensive line health in front of a long-holding Maye
Secondary depth while Carlton Davis is out

confidence.note: Six games with a fluky turnover profile and a fresh wave of line and secondary injuries.
